Long-context language models must preserve useful evidence across successive
windows. A memory reads historical key and value states before the current
attention calculation. Only after that calculation may the current key and
value states be written. This ordering prevents information from the current
window from leaking into its own prediction.

The baseline memory uses cosine similarity. Similar keys above a fixed
threshold are consolidated with a count-weighted average. A novel key occupies
an unused slot, or replaces the oldest slot when the memory is full.

The probabilistic memory uses directional statistics to decide whether a key
belongs to an existing slot. The slot is an index, while each write retains its
original key and value as an individual record. Retrieval first routes to a
small number of slots and then reranks their original records.

Perplexity is computed on one-token-ahead targets while windows are processed
sequentially. The native model cache is disabled, making external memory the
only state carried from one window to the next.
